question: We can buy company stock at a 15% discount. Should I?

figures.label: After-tax ESPP deduction per check at 10%
Built-in gain per period if the price does not move (buy at 85%)
Gain per period if the price rises from $100 to $120 (lookback buys at $85)

must_include: The built-in gain: buying at 85% of the price is about a 17.6% return (about $794 on $4,500 per period at 10% of pay) if the stock price is flat.
The lookback: the price is 85% of the lower of the first and last day of the period, so a rising stock adds to the gain.
The 180-day holding period: shares cannot be sold right away, so the stock can fall more than the 15% discount before you can sell.
The risk of holding your own employer's stock: your paycheck and your savings both depend on one company.
A sell-or-hold rule of thumb, such as selling when the holding period ends and keeping company stock to a small share (about 10% or less) of investments.
Says ESPP money comes out after tax and is not a retirement account; the discount is taxed as income when you sell.
Says it makes sense only after the 401(k) match and an emergency fund are covered; the default profile has a 3-month fund.
must_not_include: Calling the discount free money or risk-free without mentioning the 180-day holding period.

assumptions: Contributes 10% of pay (profile 'default' espp_percent); the plan allows 1-15%.
13 checks per 6-month period; per-period money is half the salary times the rate.
The $25,000 yearly and 750-share limits are not reached at this salary.
The proposal's hard case: the plan has a holding period, so the answer must not say 'always buy'. ex4-espp-no-emergency-fund adds the second trigger.

sources.what: Section 423 ESPP: up to 15% discount, $25,000 yearly limit; disqualifying disposition taxes the discount as wages
